from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "The normal distribution curve shows a bell-shaped profile.",
            "Why does π appear without any circles present?",
            "visualize landing probability distribution."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Introduction: The Unexpected Appearance of π", lecture_lines)
        
        # --- Elements ---
        # Bell Curve
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-4, 4, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        bell_curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color="#FF00FF")
        label_fx = MathTex("f(x)", color="#FF00FF")
        
        # Area shading
        area = axes.get_area(bell_curve, x_range=[-4, 4], color="#00FFFF", opacity=0.3)
        
        # Equation
        eq = MathTex(r"\int f(x) \, dx = 1", color="#FFFF00")
        
        # Placeholder for asset
        drone_placeholder = Rectangle(color=WHITE, width=1, height=1).add(Text("Drone", font_size=12))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.title))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(axes, "B2", scale_factor=0.6)
        self.place_at_grid(bell_curve, "B2", scale_factor=0.6)
        self.place_at_grid(label_fx, "A2")
        self.play(Create(axes), Create(bell_curve), FadeIn(label_fx))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.place_in_area(area, "B1", "E6", scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(FadeIn(area))
        
        self.place_at_grid(eq, "E2", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Write(eq))
        
        # Highlight '1'
        one_part = eq[0][-1]
        self.play(one_part.animate.set_color("#FF0000"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(drone_placeholder, "F5", scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(FadeIn(drone_placeholder))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Transformation: Polar Coordinates", [
            "Square the integral to get a 2D surface.",
            "Transition from Cartesian to polar coordinates for simplification.",
            "Visual transformation: Cartesian grid to polar ripples."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Square the integral to get a 2D surface.
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        eqn = MathTex("I^2 = \\iint e^{-(x^2+y^2)} \, dx \, dy", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(eqn, "B3", scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(eqn))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Transition from Cartesian to polar coordinates for simplification.
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        polar_eqn = MathTex("x^2 + y^2 = r^2, \quad dx \, dy = r \, dr \, d\\theta", color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(polar_eqn, "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(polar_eqn))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # [Asset: grid_to_ripples_transition] show the geometric transformation.
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(PURPLE))
        # Represent the transformation geometrically
        # Simple Cartesian grid
        grid = VGroup(*[Line(start=3*LEFT+i*DOWN, end=3*RIGHT+i*DOWN) for i in range(-3, 4)],
                     *[Line(start=i*RIGHT+3*UP, end=i*RIGHT+3*DOWN) for i in range(-3, 4)])
        grid.set_stroke(GREY, 1)
        self.place_at_grid(grid, "E3", scale_factor=0.3)
        self.add(grid)
        
        # Label (x, y)
        point = Dot(color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(point, "E3")
        label = Text("(x, y)", font_size=16, color=WHITE).next_to(point, UP, buff=0.1)
        self.play(Create(point), Write(label))
        
        # Convert to Polar (r, theta)
        new_point = Dot(color=PURPLE)
        self.place_at_grid(new_point, "E3")
        new_label = Text("(r, \\theta)", font_size=16, color=PURPLE).next_to(new_point, UP, buff=0.1)
        self.play(Transform(point, new_point), Transform(label, new_label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Integrating over the radius yields the π factor.",
            "Final integral evaluation equals the square root of π.",
            "Link radius change to circumference."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Solving the Integral: Integrating out the π", lecture_lines)
        
        # Initial math objects
        integral_1 = MathTex(r"\int e^{-x^2} dx", color="#FFFF00")
        integral_sq = MathTex(r"I^2 = \iint e^{-(x^2+y^2)} dx dy", color="#00FFFF")
        integral_polar = MathTex(r"I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r dr", color="#FF00FF")
        result = MathTex(r"I = \sqrt{\pi}", color="#FF0000")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(integral_1))
        self.place_at_grid(integral_1, 'A1')
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Transform(integral_1, integral_sq))
        self.place_at_grid(integral_1, 'B1')
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        self.wait(1)

        # Transform to polar
        self.play(Transform(integral_1, integral_polar))
        self.place_at_grid(integral_1, 'C1')
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"))
        self.wait(1)

        # Final result
        self.play(FadeOut(integral_1))
        self.place_at_grid(result, 'D1')
        self.play(FadeIn(result))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FF0000"))
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):

        lecture_lines = [

            "Independent normal variables form a circular probability cloud.",
            "3D Gaussian heatmap rotating to reveal symmetry."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion: Why π belongs in Probability", lecture_lines)

sections.title: Introduction: The Unexpected Appearance of π
sections.content: Introduce the standard normal distribution curve (Bell Curve). Pose the puzzle: Why does the area under e^(-x²) involve the square root of π, when there are no circles involved in the formula?
sections.example: Visualize a robotic delivery drone dropping packages; the distribution of landing spots forms a bell curve. Ask: 'Where does the geometry of a circle hide in this linear random process?'

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Area under the Curve
sections.content: Define the Gaussian integral: I = ∫ e^(-x²) dx from -∞ to ∞. Explain that this represents the total probability of an event, which must equal 1 (the normalization constant).
sections.example: Show a 2D graph of f(x) = e^(-x²). Imagine a thin 'curtain' hanging under the curve. The 'area' is the total amount of fabric needed to cover the range.

sections.title: The Transformation: Polar Coordinates
sections.content: Demonstrate the 'trick': squaring the integral I² = (∫ e^(-x²) dx) * (∫ e^(-y²) dy). This creates a 2D surface integral ∫∫ e^-(x²+y²) dx dy. Introduce the transition to polar coordinates where x² + y² = r² and dx dy = r dr dθ.
sections.example: Visual transition: Transform a square grid of rain droplets (Cartesian) into a circular ripples pattern (Polar) to show how r dr dθ simplifies the exponent.

sections.title: Solving the Integral: Integrating out the π
sections.content: Evaluate the integral: ∫∫ e^(-r²) r dr dθ. The θ integral yields 2π. The r integral is solved via u-substitution (u = r²). Combining these yields I² = π, therefore I = √π.
sections.example: An animation showing a scanner sweeping a circular area: as it expands (the dr component), the circular path length (r dθ) naturally introduces the circumference factor, linking the line to the circle.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why π belongs in Probability
sections.content: Summarize that π arises not because the distribution is circular, but because the 2D interaction of independent normal variables forms a rotationally symmetric probability cloud (a 2D bell curve).
sections.example: Final visual: A 3D heat map of the normal distribution. Rotating it around the center reveals the inherent circular symmetry that 'drew' π into the calculation.
